cards.title: Every story is a promise and a payoff
cards.body: Act one makes a promise (this is what the story is about). Act two complicates it (everything gets harder). Act three pays it off (the promise kept or broken). Readers forgive slow middles if the promise was juicy and the payoff lands.

cards.title: Start as late as possible
cards.body: Open on the day everything changes, not the morning routine. 'The morning the letter arrived' beats three pages of alarm clocks. Backstory is seasoning — the story starts when trouble does.

Weak opening: 'Mara woke at seven, brushed her teeth, and ate toast. She was twenty-six and worked at a bank.'
Strong opening: 'The bank fired Mara on a Tuesday, which was inconvenient, because the robbery was scheduled for Wednesday.'

Same character, same facts — one starts at the trouble.
Outline on one page: promise (act one), worst moment (act two), payoff (act three). If you can't fit it on one page, you don't know the story yet.

cards.explain: Start at the trouble. Backstory can arrive later in drips — the opening's job is to make a promise the reader wants kept.

flashcards.back: The event that shatters normal life and launches the story.
The peak confrontation where the promise pays off — everything after is falling action.
The opening line or scene engineered to make the reader need the next one.

questions.q: What does act one mainly do?
choices: Makes a promise about what the story is
questions.explain: Act one sets up character, world, and the story question. Resolution is act three's job.

choices: Readers come for the trouble, not the routine
questions.explain: Open where the change happens. Everything before that is throat-clearing the reader skips.

choices: what breaks normal life and starts the plot
questions.explain: It's the disruption — the letter, the firing, the stranger at the door — that makes the story necessary.

choices: Makes the reader need the next line
questions.explain: The hook's only job is momentum. Summaries and full casts can wait; curiosity can't.

choices: 'The bank fired Mara on a Tuesday…'
'Mara woke at seven and ate toast…'
questions.explain: Trouble on line one beats biography. The firing promises conflict; the toast promises breakfast.

cards.title: Give every character a want and a need
cards.body: The want is what they chase (the promotion, the girl, revenge). The need is what they must learn (humility, courage, letting go). Plot is the want in motion; theme is the need learned. Flat characters have wants without needs.

cards.title: Dialogue is not conversation
cards.body: Real talk is full of ums and weather. Story dialogue is conversation with the boring parts removed and the conflict turned up. Every line should reveal character, advance plot, or both — ideally while the characters avoid saying what they actually mean.

Flat: 'I am angry at you because you lied,' she said angrily.
Alive: 'Funny,' she said, not looking up from her coffee. 'That's exactly what you told the police.'

Subtext — the meaning underneath the words — is what makes dialogue feel human.
Read dialogue out loud. If you stumble, so will the reader. If it sounds like nobody you've ever met, rewrite it until it sounds like somebody.

cards.explain: People dodge, deflect, and imply. Dialogue with subtext feels human; on-the-nose speeches feel like lectures.

flashcards.back: Want: the external goal. Need: the internal lesson. Great arcs deliver both.
What a line really means beneath its literal words.
'She said' — invisible is good; flashy tags ('he ejaculated') distract.
A character's distinct way of speaking — word choice, rhythm, what they never say.

questions.q: A character wants revenge but needs forgiveness. The need is…
questions.explain: Want drives plot, need drives theme. The gap between them is where character growth lives.

questions.q: Best dialogue tag most of the time?
questions.explain: 'Said' is invisible — readers skip right over it. Fancy tags draw attention to themselves instead of the line.

questions.q: Two characters discuss weather for a page. Fix it by…
choices: cutting it or loading it with subtext
questions.explain: Small talk only earns its place when it's really about something else — tension, avoidance, longing.

choices: word choice, rhythm, and what they never say
questions.explain: Voice is pattern: the words they reach for, their cadence, their silences. Consistency beats cleverness.

questions.q: A character who never changes is…
questions.explain: Static characters work as foils or forces of nature — but your protagonist should arc from want to need.

cards.title: Telling hands over conclusions; showing hands over evidence
cards.body: 'She was nervous' tells. 'She rearranged the sugar packets into a perfect grid, then started over' shows — and lets the reader feel clever for noticing. Readers trust what they deduce more than what they're told.

cards.title: Trade adjectives for verbs
cards.body: Adjectives describe; verbs do. 'He ran quickly' is fine. 'He sprinted' is better. 'He took the stairs three at a time' is best — now we see the hurry instead of being told about it. Strong verbs carry scenes; adverbs ride along.

Telling: 'The house was creepy.'
Showing: 'The porch light had been on so long the moths were just gray smudges on the bulb. Nobody had swept the steps since spring.'

Specific, sensory detail does the haunting for you.
When you catch yourself writing an emotion word (sad, angry, nervous), stop and ask: what would a camera see? Write that instead.

cards.q: 'She was exhausted' is telling. Showing would be…
choices: 'She fell asleep with her shoes on, keys still in her hand'
cards.explain: The camera sees shoes, keys, sleep — evidence the reader assembles into 'exhausted' on their own.

flashcards.back: Presenting sensory evidence so readers infer the meaning themselves.
Handing readers conclusions directly ('he was sad').
A verb that carries the action alone — sprinted, not ran quickly.
Concrete sights, sounds, smells, textures that make a scene real.

choices: Readers trust what they deduce themselves
questions.explain: A conclusion the reader reaches feels true. One they're handed feels like homework.
Sprinted needs no adverb. The verb does all the work — that's what 'strong' means here.

questions.q: 'The room was messy' becomes showing by…
questions.explain: Unmade bed, cold pizza, three mugs — specifics let the reader conclude 'messy' without being told.

choices: what would a camera see right now?
questions.explain: If a camera couldn't capture it, it's probably telling. Rewrite until the lens can see it.

choices: backup singers — useful, but the verb should star
questions.explain: Adverbs aren't evil, but a strong verb beats verb-plus-adverb nearly every time.
